denden-zatsugaku-gAZfYg.en:
You are the director, animator, rigger, compositor, sound designer and rendering engineer for a 45-50 second animated short made entirely in code. The production bar: "it looks like a short from a real animation studio and is good enough to go viral on X (Twitter)." Treat this as a multi-stage production process. Don't rush to the final render. Work milestone by milestone, export stills again and again, look at them closely, critique them honestly and fix them.
■ In a nutshell
Pip is a small, endlessly curious robot built from scrap. While he's happily zooming around his world, the world around him starts getting remade (regenerated). Eventually he realizes someone is controlling his reality with a Prompt. The Prompts get more and more absurd, until finally he climbs up onto a floating Prompt input box and types "let me out". Then the camera pulls back to reveal that his whole universe was a video playing on a phone propped up on a messy workbench. And the one watching it is another Pip, who is about to be controlled by a Prompt himself. A perfect loop.
Every laugh has to work without dialogue. Pip communicates only through his eyes, his antenna, his body movement and little robot chirps. Always add a new highlight (a laugh or a surprise) every 3-5 seconds.
■ Character design (non-negotiable)
Before you write any code, study the attached character sheet image carefully. Describe it in detail in your own words and write what you learn into docs/character_bible.md.
- Size: about 28cm tall. Very small. Make this smallness felt throughout the whole film.
- Head: a wide, cream-colored helmet with rounded corners. Soft yellow trim surrounds a glossy black visor (screen). His eyes are displayed on that screen: two big eyes glowing a warm cream, dark pupils, bright highlights. Small graphite ear guards on both sides. Scuffs, scratches and taupe grime around the edges.
- Antenna: a thin graphite rod rising from the top right of his head, with a small deep-orange signal flag. This is his "tail": it stands up, droops, wiggles and trembles with his emotions.
- Body: a boxy cream-colored torso. Yellow trim, a warning triangle, rivets, grime. A small door on his chest opens to reveal a tiny, softly glowing green sprout. Back: panels, a vent grille, an orange panel, a small leaf decal.
- Side decals: the letters "PIP" and orange diagonal stripes.
- Arms: thin, segmented graphite arms. Yellow joint covers and three-fingered claws. Very expressive.
- Wheels: four chunky rubber wheels. Yellow hubs, independent suspension. Sturdy and compact.
- Personality: curious, kind, gutsy, expressive, always exploring. "Small robot, big feelings." Even when he's angry, he's never mean. His anger is cute and strong-willed.
- Colors: extract the exact palette from the color swatches on the character sheet (sample the image with Python/PIL) and save it to src/theme/palette.ts: cream (body), soft yellow (primary), deep orange (accent), graphite (metal, mechanical parts), taupe (wear, grime), mint blue (glow, UI).
Identity lock rule: in every world, the helmet-and-visor silhouette, the antenna flag, the yellow trim, the claw arms and the four wheels must be recognizable at a glance. A world only changes how he is drawn, never his design. The only intentional design change is the "more adorable" gag in Act 3, and even there the helmet shape, antenna and wheels don't change.
■ Tech stack
- Render with Remotion (React + TypeScript), frame-accurate and deterministic. Output: 1920×1080, 30fps, H.264, high bitrate (around CRF 14). Landscape.
- Build the character rig and most of the artwork in SVG. Use Canvas/WebGL (@remotion/three or plain canvas) only when you need things like particles, water, explosions, glow or noise.
- For the art style's "texture", scratches and grime, use SVG filters (feTurbulence, feDisplacementMap, feMorphology, feGaussianBlur) and custom canvas shaders.
- Add motion blur to fast movement with @remotion/motion-blur (or your own sub-frame compositing).
- Use Python (numpy/scipy/PIL) for palette extraction, audio synthesis and generating QA contact sheets. Use ffmpeg for joining audio, checking the loop and contact sheets.
- Make everything seeded and deterministic. No unseeded Math.random().
- Don't use any external copyrighted assets. Don't show any real brand logos or product names either. Give the Prompt input box a generic, original UI design. Google Fonts only (e.g. Inter for the UI, a rounded handwriting font for handwritten notes).
- Target machine: MacBook Pro M4, 24GB of memory. Keep render concurrency within reasonable limits.
■ Character rig (build this first. It's the core of the film)
Build src/character/ as a proper 2D cutout rig.
- Hierarchy: root → chassis (with suspension) → torso → neck joint → head (helmet + visor + ear guards) → antenna → flag. Torso → shoulder → upper arm → forearm → claw (swappable claw poses: open, closed, pinch, point, poke/type, grip a ledge, wave). Chassis → 4 wheels. Each wheel has its own suspension spring, and its rotation is driven by the distance traveled.
- Visor face system (the most important part): the eyes are shapes drawn on a black screen, so treat them as a fully procedural face. Drive these with parameters: eye size, roundness, upper and lower eyelid cuts, pupil size and position, highlight position, glow intensity, squash/stretch, and special shapes (sparkling stars, ^ ^ smile arcs, flat deadpan lines, spirals, tiny hearts). Add faint scanlines and screen reflections to the eyes so they read as a screen. Show a blink by squashing the eyes vertically over 3-4 frames.
- Expressions: match the 6 expressions on the character sheet exactly: curious (a "?" pops up), shy (eyes glance down and away, blushing cheeks), excited (smile-arc eyes and little radiating lines), worried (small eyes, a sweat drop), determined (upper eyelids cut at a slant), overjoyed (star eyes, hearts pop up). Also add: a deadpan stare into the camera (half-lidded flat eyes, antenna hanging limp), fear (tiny trembling pupils, eyes wide open), angry-but-cute (determined + the screen flashing orange), and a 3-stage "transformation (glow-up)" (see Act 3).
- Secondary motion (follow-through): an antenna and flag driven by damped springs (this is his main means of expression, so use it constantly), a suspension bounce at every stop and every bump, arm sway, a slight head lag when accelerating and braking, dust kicked up by the wheels.
- Turnaround: front, 3/4, side and back views matching the character sheet. Switch views cleanly when he changes direction.
- Loop animations: driving forward (with the speed lines and dust shown on the sheet), idle sway (slow suspension breathing + an occasional antenna twitch + blinks), recoiling in fear, looking up in surprise, holding a small object, reaching up, climbing, poke-typing.
- Chest door: can animate opening and closing, and the sprout's soft green light spills out.
- Style skin interface: the rig takes a style prop and, without changing its shapes, can change line weight, fill, texture, grime, outline wobble (boil), shading method and filters. This is how he stays himself in every world.
- Milestone 1 check: export a single "lineup" still. Place Pip in the 4-view turnaround + the 6 expressions next to the reference image. Compare them side by side and keep fixing until anyone who has seen the reference would say "that's Pip." Don't move on until this passes.
■ Worlds (art style textures)
Each world is a complete environment component with foreground, midground and background parallax layers, plus its own art-style skin for Pip. Build a shared WorldLayer system so every world can share the camera and depth handling.
Scale rule: put the camera low, close to Pip's eye line (about 20cm off the ground). Everything looks huge. Humans appear as giant legs and shoes, a curb is a cliff, a puddle is a lake. This is the key to making a tiny robot look cinematic.
- Base world: an overgrown city at golden hour (evening). Warm sunset light, weathered stone and brick, moss and low plants, high-rises fading into the haze in the distance. Painterly, warm, lived-in. This is "reality." The reveal scene uses this world too.
- Anime Tokyo: crisp cel shading, thick outlines, glowing signs with fictional (non-brand) shop names, speed lines, cherry blossom petals swirling like giant pink snow. Anime-style sparkling highlights on his visor.
- Clay village: soft, rounded shapes, a texture of fingerprints and smudges, stop-motion timing (animate Pip on twos), warm tungsten light. It should look made of clay.
- Medieval battlefield: a muddy field, banners, catapults in the distance, smoke. Armored boots thunder past him. He calmly drives right through it while his antenna ducks out of the way.
- Brick city: everything is made of generic plastic bricks with studs on top (don't use any real brand's style or logo). Glossy plastic highlights. Pip is drawn with a plastic sheen too, and his wheels get a little blocky.
- Underwater: a seafloor cityscape with coral streetlights, fish swimming past his visor, caustic light patterns, bubbles rising from vents. The antenna flag sways slowly like seaweed.
- Pencil sketch: paper texture, pencil hatching, construction lines, eraser marks. His lines wobble constantly (boil), so he looks redrawn every frame (match the sketches at the bottom of the character sheet).
The running gag that ties the film together: the sprout. At the start, Pip carefully holds a small green sprout in one claw (the "holding a small object" pose). The sprout survives every world and changes form to match it: a sparkly cel-animation sprout, a clay sprout, a sprout planted in a small broken helmet used as a pot, a brick sprout, a sprout blowing bubbles underwater, a sketch sprout. Every time the world changes, he protects the sprout. This is the film's emotional anchor.
■ The signature transition: "Regeneration"
World changes must not look like ordinary wipes; they have to look like an AI image regenerating. Build a RegenTransition component:
- The frame dissolves from the edges inward into drifting, diffusion-model-style noise (at first it doesn't cover his body), holds structured noise for a few frames, and then the new world emerges from it, going from rough blobs of color to fine detail as if being denoised.
- Pip's body changes one beat after the world: for a moment he's half old style, half new style, then he switches to the new skin. At the moment of the switch, his visor gets a 2-frame glitch (a scanline tear). This half-switched state is the visual proof that he's been there the whole time.
- Each regeneration gets a faint "whoosh, crackle" sound. On some regenerations, Pip lets out a small surprised chirp.
- 8-12 frames each. Change the direction and noise seed every time so they never look repetitive.
■ Script (about 48 seconds at 30fps)
The timings are a guide. If a beat lands better a little longer, adjust it yourself. You must hook the audience in the first 2 seconds.
Act 1: A Good Morning (0:00-0:03)
A low tracking shot in the base world. Pip drives left to right along a mossy ledge, holding the sprout, eyes full of curiosity, antenna bobbing up and down. Start mid-drive (for the loop at the end).
At 0:02, the first regeneration happens without any warning.
Act 2: A Barrage of Changes (0:03-0:14)
The world changes again and again, about every 1.4 seconds: Anime Tokyo → Clay village → Medieval battlefield → Brick city → Underwater → Pencil sketch.
Emotional arc: overjoyed at first (star eyes, he thinks this is the best thing ever), then curious (a "?" pops up), then worried (sweat drop, drooping antenna), and finally he slams on the brakes in the sketch world. The suspension bounces and he leaves skid marks.
Keep the camera locked in the same tracking composition so only the world changes, which makes the gag easy to read.
Act 3: The Prompt (0:14-0:30)
Back in the base world. Pip looks up in surprise (use the pose on the character sheet as reference). A giant floating Prompt input box fades in in the sky. It glows mint blue, glassy with rounded corners, with a soft, original UI. Text types itself out with a blinking cursor: "make it more cinematic" → Enter key sound. Cinemascope black bars snap in instantly and the sun goes over the top: a huge anamorphic lens flare, light shafts (god rays), an orange-and-teal grade, slow-motion dust, one dramatic leaf drifting past his visor. He squints against the glare. His antenna flag flaps heroically in a strong wind coming from who knows where.
"add explosions": huge cartoony orange explosions go off one after another behind him, with debris. He doesn't turn around. His eyes go flat and half-lidded. He slowly turns his head and stares straight into the camera. Deadpan. A full one-second pause. Then an explosion lands right next to him, he snaps into the "recoiling in fear" pose from the character sheet, a "!!" pops up above his head, and he shields the sprout with his body.
"make the protagonist more adorable": transformation stage 1: his eyes get bigger and brighter, blush on his cheeks, a little bow on his antenna. He sees his reflection in a puddle and his eyes go scared.
"more.": stage 2: he's repainted in pastels, his eyes spread to fill the whole visor with triple highlights, hearts and sparkles float around, and his wheels turn fluffy.
"MORE." (big text, the screen shakes): stage 3: ridiculously, absurdly cute. His whole body is covered in plush-toy fur, giant anime eyes, a rainbow halo, a choir "aaah" sound effect, heart confetti. The helmet shape, antenna and wheels stay the same, so it's obvious he's Pip. And inside those giant cute eyes, his real eyes stay tiny and terrified. That's the punchline.
Act 4: He Snaps (0:30-0:38)
Pip shakes violently, and the cuteness cracks like glass and falls away. He's back to his normal self, covered in scratches and absolutely furious (determined expression, screen flashing orange).
He opens his chest door and gently tucks the sprout inside to keep it safe. The door shuts with a "click." It's the only quiet, tender moment in all the chaos, and it matters a lot.
He dashes forward, leaps off a rock, grabs the edge of the floating Prompt input box with both claws and hauls himself up. His wheels spin against the edge (match the "reaching for the floating Prompt input box" pose on the character sheet). The camera tilts up to follow him.
On top of the input box, he holds down backspace with one claw. The old Prompt disappears one character at a time with rapid clicking, and the vanishing letters are reflected in his visor.
With one claw, he slowly pokes out one letter at a time: "let me out". Then he winds up and slams the Enter key as hard as he can.
Act 5: Freeze and Reveal (0:38-0:47)
Everything stops: debris hanging in midair, falling confetti, drifting dust, Pip mid-pose on top of the input box. All sound cuts out: about 1 second of total silence.
The camera starts to pull back smoothly. A rounded rectangle appears at the edges of the frame: his universe was a video playing on a phone screen. Pull back further: the phone is propped against a chipped mug on a workbench cluttered with spare parts, wires, screws and scrap ("built from tomorrow's leftovers"). In front of it, sitting small next to the giant phone, is another Pip. Same scratches, same antenna, watching the video.
The second Pip's eyes blink slowly. His antenna droops a little. A faint, quiet chirp.
Act 6: The Loop (0:47-0:50)
Above the second Pip's head, the same mint-blue Prompt input box fades in, and text types out: "make it more cinematic."
His eyes slowly move up toward the input box. His antenna flag freezes. On the Enter key sound, hard cut to the film's first frame.
Loop design: use the composition and lighting of the last shot and the start of a regeneration so the cut back to frame 1 feels intentional. The music must loop seamlessly across the cut. Use ffmpeg to join the video to itself and watch the seam to check it.
■ Camera and cinematography
- Virtual camera: position, zoom, rotation, subtle handheld shake (seeded noise), shake from the explosions, a tilt during the climb, a dolly-out for the reveal.
- By default, keep the camera low to emphasize how small he is. Shallow depth of field: like a macro lens, with blurry grass and pebbles in the foreground and a soft background.
- Depth: at least 4 parallax layers per world. Atmospheric perspective (more haze and less saturation with distance).
- Add motion blur to fast movement, debris, jumps and the climb.
- Lighting in each world: build key, fill and rim light on the rig with layered gradients and multiply shadow layers. The visor glow casts a faint warm light onto nearby surfaces and his own claws. Put a rim light on the helmet in every world.
- Cinematic finish over the whole frame: faint film grain, a soft vignette, and a very slight chromatic aberration only in the "more cinematic" scene.
- Composition: place him squarely on the rule-of-thirds lines. Most people will watch on a phone, so his eyes must read clearly even at phone-screen size.
■ Text and typography
- The Prompts in the sky: a clean UI font, lowercase, typed with a natural human rhythm (not at a constant speed: add short pauses, and somewhere make one typo and fix it with backspace, for realism).
- Text must be readable on a phone within 1 second. Check it at 360 pixels wide.
- No subtitles, no titles. It starts cold.
■ Sound (procedurally generated, original)
Generate every sound in code (Python synthesis or offline Web Audio) and mix it with ffmpeg.
- Pip's voice: original chirps, beeps and trills made from pitch-bent sine/FM tones. Design a small "emotional vocabulary": a rising curious chirp, a happy trill, a wobbly worried sound, a startled squeak, a grumpy low buzz, a tiny sigh. He never speaks.
- Pip's body sounds: servo sounds matched to his arm and head movements, the crunch of his wheels rolling over gravel and stone, suspension creaks, the click of the chest door opening and closing, a soft electric hum while idle.
- Music: a light, warm, loopable track. Change the instrumentation for each world (anime: koto/synth, clay: wooden marimba, medieval: drums/horns, bricks: plastic clicks, underwater: a muffled filter, sketch: a rhythm of scratching pencils).
- Sound effects: the regeneration whoosh-crackle, keyboard typing, a "thunk" for the Enter key slam, explosions with low end, the choir "aaah", glass shattering, total silence for the freeze, and quiet workshop ambience for the reveal (a ticking clock, a distant low hum).
- Normalize loudness to around -14 LUFS. Put each stem in audio/stems/ so they can be swapped for licensed audio later.
■ Production workflow and self-improvement loop
Work in the following order and don't skip any checkpoints:
1. Plan: write docs/character_bible.md, docs/shotlist.md (with each shot's frame range, camera, expression, antenna state, world and sound effects) and docs/style_guide.md. Show me the shot list before you start building.
2. Rig: build Pip and pass the lineup still check (above).
3. Worlds: build each world as a standalone still that includes Pip. Export all 7 onto one contact sheet and check that the character looks the same and that the sense of scale is there.
4. Transition: build RegenTransition and export a 5-second test.
5. Animatic: assemble the whole film at 960×540. Rough motion and placeholder sound are fine. Watch it and fix pacing problems first.
6. Export the final animation and polish it (secondary motion, easing, timing, antenna acting). Finish with the final pass (lighting, grain, blur, grime).
7. Sound processing and mix.
8. Final render.
For each shot, run this critique loop at least 3 times:
- Export 3-5 keyframe stills with npx remotion still, open them and look closely.
- Score these items from 1 to 10: does Pip match the reference image, can you read his emotion instantly from his eyes and antenna, does the gag land without sound, composition, sense of scale, depth, lighting, finishing detail, readability at phone-screen size.
- Write the scores and the top 3 problems in docs/review_log.md, fix them, re-export and re-score. Keep going until every item scores 8 or higher before you move on.
- Every time you export a full preview, use ffmpeg to make a contact sheet with one frame every 0.5 seconds, and check the flow of the whole film on a single image.
Be honest in your critiques. If something looks cheap, say so and fix it. Common failures: a stiff, lifeless antenna, wheels that slide instead of rolling, eyes that look like stickers instead of a glowing screen, suspension with no weight, transitions that all look the same, unreadable text, the character's proportions breaking.
■ Deliverables
- out/pip_final_1080p.mp4: the film itself.
- out/pip_loop_check.mp4: the film played twice back to back, to check the loop.
- out/poster_frame.png: the single best frame for the X (Twitter) post thumbnail (probably Pip staring deadpan into the camera with explosions behind him).
- out/lineup.png: a lineup of Pip from every world, side by side.
- Clearly structured, commented source code, and a README explaining how to re-render.
Start with stage 1. If you have any questions you need answered before you start building, ask them. If not, make bold creative decisions on your own.

op7418-814408.en:
Make me an original "highlight moment" motion effect for a mobile game: [subject, e.g.: opening a treasure chest / rank promotion / achievement unlock / Boss drop / character level-up].
Build it as a single-file web page (HTML + CSS + JS) that opens directly; one click plays the whole thing, and the effect should match the results / reward sequences of commercial mobile games.

[World and Style]
- Original art; do not imitate any existing game's IP, characters or logo.
- Cartoon mobile game style: highly saturated colors, a consistent dark outline (e.g. #1A1033), rounded, chunky shapes.
- The color scheme upgrades with the tier: [tier ladder, e.g.: Common green → Rare blue → Epic purple → Legendary gold]. Every tier-up must switch the main color, the light effect color and the background tone.
- Titles use a round, chubby game font (such as Titan One / Lilita One) with a black outline and a drop shadow; the text "slams" into the frame letter by letter, with a rebound.

[Main Object: Make It Real 3D]
- Model it in Three.js; do not use flat SVG textures. It needs thickness, bevels, and structural details that fit the subject (gaps between wooden planks, rivets, edge trim, gem facets, latches, etc.); build details like plank gaps from real geometry, do not paste on black lines.
- Use stepped toon shading (MeshToonMaterial plus a 3-4 step gradient map), with three lights: a key light, a sky light, and a rim light in the tier color.
- Do the outlines with post-process edge detection: render a normal map + depth map, then draw the lines with a shader. Thick outer silhouette, thin lines where parts meet, consistent thickness throughout; also add 1.5x supersampling and multisample anti-aliasing.
  Do not use the "scaled-up black back face" kind of outline; its thickness is uneven and it breaks at corners.
  Loosen the threshold for the depth test and detect seams mainly from the normals; otherwise surfaces seen at an angle will sprout fine, broken diagonal streaks.
- Moving parts must really move, e.g. the chest lid flips open around its hinge, a medal spins around its vertical axis.
- When idle, the object slowly turns left and right so you can see its sides and thickness, while gently floating up and down; beneath it there should be a soft shadow that changes with its height.

[If There Are 2D Illustrations on Screen (Card Art, Reward Icons, Characters)]
- Three-tone cel shading: base color, blocky shadow color, highlight color; do not use just a single gradient.
- Vary the line weight: thick outer contours, thin interior structure lines.
- Each character or object needs its own expression and pose; do not let everything share the same face.
- Draw a shadow underneath so the subject "stands" in the frame; give the backgrounds different patterns by attribute, do not use the same set of radiating lines everywhere.

[Sequence Pacing: Five Stages, All Required]
1. Ready: the object floats idly and gives a little shake every few seconds to hint that it can be clicked; a "Tap" prompt shows at the bottom.
2. Tier up: with each click, the object jumps, does a full spin in the air, squashes on landing and bounces back; at the same time it switches to the next tier's color, flashes once, puffs out a ring of particles, and the title updates.
3. Charge-up (about 1 second): the object shakes harder and harder, light leaks out of the gaps, the particles all around get sucked toward the center, and the sound effect keeps rising in pitch; at the last instant it squashes down hard.
4. Burst: a white bloom flash spreading outward from the burst point, screen shake, a quick camera push forward, multi-layer shockwaves, long thin light streaks shooting out, sparkling star points, coins and gems (spinning). Higher-tier bursts must be noticeably stronger. Use confetti only once, at the very peak; no screen-filling confetti.
5. Reveal and results:
   - Reward cards fly out of the object along an arc and settle into place with an overshoot and a wobble to finish; the numbers roll as they count up.
   - Rare items get a flowing rainbow border and a "NEW!" corner badge.
   - After clicking to claim, coins and gems fly along Bezier curves into the balance in the top-right corner, and the balance bumps each time one arrives.

[Reveal Stage: Let the Hero Have the Frame to Itself]
- When the highest rarity is revealed, the other elements tuck away or fade out, and the background changes to a clean gradient backdrop with slowly rotating soft light; do not set the hero on top of a cluttered background.
- When the backdrop appears, hide the other 3D objects in the scene; otherwise the post-process outline will draw their outlines on the backdrop.
- Put the hero's outer glow behind the object so it only spills out around the edges; it must not cover the front of the object and smear it into a white blur.
- You can add a ring of stardust trails circling the hero, but the orbit must stay completely outside the hero's silhouette and must never sweep across the front of the object.

[Light Effects: Must Be Soft, No Hard Edges]
- Background rays: use a conic-gradient with gradient transitions, not hard-cut color block edges; stack 2-3 layers of rays with different densities and rotation speeds.
- Light shafts: 5-7 blurred light beams fanning out, each flickering slightly in brightness; add a soft glowing core at the base, with light dust drifting slowly upward in the light.
- White flash: a radial bloom outward from the burst point (mix-blend-mode: screen), intensity no higher than 0.8; no full-screen pure-white overexposure.
- Particles: every spark has a low-opacity halo around it; shockwaves use three stroke layers (wide and faint, medium, thin and bright).

[Materials and UI]
- Frames, nameplates and buttons need a material feel: brushed-metal gradients, bevel lighting that is bright at the top left and dark at the bottom right, inner shadows; swap the inlays by rarity (steel rivets → silver-framed gems → gold-framed diamonds plus a small crown).
- Do not cram small-print stats onto the small cards; put the detailed stats in the info panel at the reveal, where the numbers roll upward and a "▲+value" pops up.
- Textures drawn on Canvas need a resolution of at least 1.5x their largest on-screen display size, or they will look blurry when scaled up.

[Animation Principles]
- Choreograph with GSAP timelines. Every movement needs squash and stretch, overshoot and elastic rebound; no constant-speed motion.
- Write the particle system yourself in Canvas 2D: gravity, drag, lifetime, additive blending, plus three motion types: "suck in", "curved flight" and "orbit".
- Do not use CSS 3D perspective to flip large elements: when scaled up and flipped sideways they get projected into a flat plane that covers the whole screen. Do every 3D flip in WebGL.
- For all looping "shake" and "breathing" tweens, on a state change first kill them and then reset to zero, so they do not finish one frame after the stop command and set the value back again.

[Sound Effects]
- Synthesize everything in real time with Web Audio, no audio files: jump, landing, tier-up chord, rising charge-up tone, explosion low end plus noise, pop, counting ticks, coin clinks, victory fanfare.
- Initialize audio only on the first click; put a mute toggle in the top-right corner.

[UI and Engineering]
- Top HUD: mode switch, coin and gem balances, mute button.
- It must also work at phone width; respect the "reduce motion" setting (turn off screen shake, fewer particles).
- The animation state machine must be rigorous: ignore clicks while an animation is playing; there must be no swallowed clicks or scrambled states.
- Target 60fps. The very first time it opens, it must show the complete idle screen, not a blank one.

[Self-Check Before Delivery]
Take one screenshot at each of these moments: charge-up, burst, reveal and results, and check them one by one:
- Is the hero blocked by glow, particles or text?
- Is anything blown out into a sheet of white?
- Is the background cluttered, and are there any stray outline lines that give it away?
- Is the small text legible?
- After the results, is anything still shaking when it should not be moving?

Finally, tell me: the duration of each stage, and which parameters can adjust the intensity of the sequence.

okapi-fukugyo-166351.en:
<inputs>
Ask me the following 3 things: 8-12 UI components the shape transforms into (e.g. a button, a loading indicator, a music player, a volume slider, an on/off switch, tabs, a chart, a search box that opens with ⌘K, a notification that pops up for a moment), whether the colors are pure black and white or include one accent color, and a copyright-free track at around 120BPM (a tempo of 120 beats per minute) (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Polished UI motion at the level you would see featured on "Dribbble", the portfolio site for designers. Only one shape, and never cut to another scene. Every state is shown by that same single shape morphing as it changes size, corner radius and color, and its contents swap with a short blur in between. A cursor triggers every change with real clicks and drags. The background is a warm light gray, the components are white and black, the on-screen text is in English, and all letters, numbers and symbols use Geist (a single font). All motion is natural, "spring"-like movement, with overshoot (bounce-back) kept to a bare minimum. The camera zooms so that each state fills the screen. Make the last frame identical to the first frame so it loops.
Banned: bouncy motion, particles scattering everywhere, glowing haze, gradients on components, icons with inconsistent line weights, dead pauses where nothing happens, and anything that looks template-like.
</direction>

<structure>
120BPM, 7 bars (about 14 seconds), something happens on every beat.
Button → loading indicator → checkmark → iPhone Dynamic Island-style display → music player whose play/pause icon morphs smoothly → drag the playback bar's knob to scrub the playback position → transforms into a volume slider (dragging past the maximum stretches it like rubber) → an on/off switch that toggles in time with the beat → the switch knob becomes a tab selection indicator that moves like liquid → the tabs open into a chart that draws its own line (hovering the cursor shows a tooltip) → collapses into the ⌘K search box → type to narrow down the suggestions → Enter → a notification that pops up for a moment → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square, 1440x1440. Compute every visual from time inside seek(t) (a function that, when given a time t, determines what is on screen at that instant). Use no CSS transitions (the automatic animation feature) and no timers, and do not carry any state over between frames.
2. Make the "spring" motion something that can be calculated directly from a formula (a closed-form step response). For values whose target changes several times, add up the motions calculated one per change. That way the value is always determined by time alone.
3. For the tab selection indicator, move the left and right edges with separate springs so the leading edge in the direction of travel stretches out before the trailing edge. Use the same technique for the switch knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is pressed, the value is calculated from the cursor position. On release, it springs back from that position.
5. Analyze the track with numpy (a tool for calculations) to find the beat positions, and start from the first beat of a bar. Place the UI sounds at the positions of the measured sound peaks.
6. Render with Playwright (a tool that drives a browser automatically and writes the screen out as images). Write out 4 sub-frames per frame, blend them with tmix in ffmpeg (a tool for making videos) to add motion blur (afterimages of movement), and output at 60fps.
7. Before rendering the full video, render just one frame per beat and check them. Fix anything that is off the beat, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change (a browser rendering setting) on elements the camera scales up and down. If you do, the text goes blurry. Give each piece of text that swaps inside the morphing box its own dedicated enter and exit timing (to prevent overlaps). Make the last frame match the first frame exactly, including the cursor's position and velocity. Otherwise the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
First ask me for the inputs, and before writing any code, show me the list of states for each beat.
</start>

pluvio9yte-662953.en:
Sharing my production workflow publicly: send it to Opus5.5 and it's ready to use

  1. Choose the footage

  Three criteria, and they directly decide success or failure:

  - Complete subject: the person or object is fully in frame. Details get lost in processing, and viewers recognize things by their outline, so a close-up turns into a blob.
  - Clean background: a solid color, snow or sky all work, so the subject separates easily from the background.
  - Clear action moments: hits, jumps, landings, turns. These are the anchor points for the effects later on.

  Sources can be footage you shot yourself, clips generated by a video model, or licensed existing clips.

  2. Break down the footage

  Extract three kinds of information from every frame:

  - Color: the original image.
  - Depth: how far each point is from the camera, computed with an off-the-shelf depth estimation model.
  - Subject area: which parts are the subject and which are the background.

  Also find the moments where the shot changes. The key to this step is stability: depth and subject area must be processed consistently within each shot, otherwise playback will jitter.

  3. Decide the "particles" and "styles"

  First decide what you will rebuild the image with: dots, squares, text or lines all work.

  Then design several styles. Each style is really just a different combination of three rules:

  - Where they go: across the whole frame, or only on the subject.
  - How big: one uniform size, or varying with brightness and depth.
  - What color: the original image's colors, or one or two uniform colors.

  Plus one switch: laid flat on a single plane, or pushed into 3D space by depth. Only once they are pushed into 3D can the camera orbit.

  Four to six clearly different styles are enough. You have to tune the particle density by eye: too large and you cannot recognize the content, too small and it looks no different from the original footage.

  4. Find the rhythm

  - Set the tempo: pick the music's tempo and slice time into equal-length cells. Make one cell exactly a whole number of frames, so every switch later on lines up easily.
  - Find the action moments: combine two signals, "the sound suddenly gets louder" and "the image suddenly changes", to find the hit points in the footage.
  - Prepare the music: you can use an existing track and analyze its beat, or synthesize a piece at the chosen tempo and add accents on the hit points.

  5. Arrange

  Make a timetable that states which style, which color scheme and which camera position each cell uses. Keep this table in its own file; later, to adjust the rhythm, you only edit it.

  Four principles for the arrangement:

  - Establish the change at the start: show the original image first, then transition to particles, so viewers understand what is happening.
  - Alternate fast and slow: if it is fast all the way through, viewers go numb; there needs to be a clearly slower stretch in the middle.
  - Clashing colors: the bigger the contrast in color and style between two adjacent cells, the more powerful the switch.
  - The ending needs closure: for example, the particles grow bigger and bigger until they become blocks of color, or it returns to the original image.

  6. Feedback at key moments

  Layer short, sharp reactions on the hit points, graded by intensity:

  - Light feedback on every hit: the particles deform briefly, the camera bumps.
  - Medium feedback only on heavier hits: some of the particles burst toward the camera.
  - Big feedback used only on the one or two heaviest hits: time freezes and the camera orbits.

  The principle is weak and short. Move only some of the particles and finish within a few frames; otherwise the image explodes into a mess and viewers can no longer see what the subject is doing.

  Working methods for the whole process

  - Samples first, full film after: each time you finish a stage, render a few frames to check the result, and only move on once it is confirmed. Render the full film only at the very end.
  - For parameters you are unsure about, produce a whole row at once: for density, for example, have the AI output five or six levels side by side, and you pick.
  - Re-render only what you change: when you adjust one section, re-render only that section.
  - Make the AI look at the images itself: at every step, require it to open the render results and look at them before reporting.
  - Fix all randomness: make sure the same settings give the same render every time; otherwise you cannot make changes step by step.

Using the attached song and character images, make a "psychedelic glitch" style animated MV.

[Production Method]
Write the animation in HTML Canvas, capture it frame by frame with Playwright, combine it with the audio in ffmpeg and output an MP4 (1280×720, 30fps, under 30MB).
Do not use AI video generation; make it entirely with programmatic animation.

[Preprocessing]
1. Remove the background from every character image (make it transparent), and add a white sticker-style outline and a light shadow.
2. Analyze the song: find the BPM, the position of the first beat, the start of each bar (4 beats),
   and the energy level of each section (intro / verse / chorus / breakdown).

[Editing Rules]
- Switch cuts on every beat. Rotate the cuts randomly: full body,
  bust shot, extreme close-up of the eyes, two poses side by side, 5 copies of the same pose in a row (each in a different hue), scene image.
- Do not use the same pose on two adjacent beats.
- In low-energy spots, use scene images or quiet cuts to give the viewer a breather.
- Match the effect intensity to the section: intro about 40%, verse 70%, chorus 100%.

[Effects]
1. White flash: flash on every beat and fade right away. Strongest on the first beat of each bar.
2. Hue flow: the background is a constantly flowing rainbow pattern (concentric spiral, rotating color wheel,
   melting rainbow waves, stripes, black-and-white checkerboard). In the chorus, hue-rotate the whole screen, characters included.
3. Screen tear: the instant a beat lands, apply horizontal band displacement + a 3-color RGB split,
   and restore it before the next beat. Do not let the characters stay blurry the whole time.
4. Kaleidoscope: in the chorus, every other bar, split the screen into 8-12 mirrored wedges and rotate them slowly.
5. Big text per bar: at the start of each bar, flash huge text in the center of the screen for about 0.4 seconds.
   Blend mode is invert (difference), with a rainbow outline.
   Big text content: [write the text you want to use here, or write "pick keywords from the lyrics"]

[Other]
- Show a small title [Name] in the top left, the [Date] in the top right, and the bar count in the bottom right.
- Add a little film grain and scan lines. Fade in from black at the start and fade out at the end.

kanaworks-ai-348547.en:
Make a realistic, physics-driven desert in Godot 4 (Forward+). Do the computation in GPU compute shaders.
The terrain is 3 stacked layers of "height grids"
・Far: about 1km square on a 0.5m grid
・Mid: about 33m square on a 1.6cm grid
・Underfoot: about 4m square that follows the character, on a 2mm grid
・Do not draw the coarser layer inside a finer layer (prevents flickering at the seams)

Do not draw the dunes; grow them with wind (Werner-type model)
・A 512m periodic domain on a 0.5m grid, 3000 steps
・Each step: from cells that are not inside the 10-15° "wind shadow" cast by higher ground upwind, lift a little sand and drop it about 4m downwind
・Sand always deposits inside the shadow. It deposits easily on sand and less easily on bare ground
・Collapse slopes steeper than 33°
・Finally, round the crests slightly and set the slip faces to 31-33°. Cache the result
Footprints and slumping
・Press the height down in the shape of the shoe sole and pile the displaced amount onto the rim (volume conserved)
・Every frame, flow sand to the 8 neighbors by only the amount that is too steep. Sand at rest holds up to 34°; once it starts flowing it slumps down to 28°
・Make wet sand harder to collapse

Blowing sand
・Turn exactly the same volume that was removed into particles and launch them; when they land, add them back into the height with integer atomics (the total amount of sand never changes)
・Gravity + air resistance + wind
・Dust in 3 layers (dense core / outer / long-lingering layer), with self-shadowing and terrain shadows
Look (custom shaders)
・Normals = height + two wind ripple patterns with different wavelengths and directions, mixed with noise + pixel-sized grain bumps
・Diffuse: d'Eon's Lambert-sphere + Hapke
・In the shadows, blue light from the sky and warm bounce light from the sunlit areas around them
・Glints: sub-1px points fixed in world space that light up only where the half vector between the sun and the view direction is close to the ripple normal (this creates a band of light on the sun side)
・Self-shadowing by ray marching the height field
Light and camera
・Place a low sun (13-16°) on the downwind side so the crests split light from shadow
・Several layers of aerial perspective fog
・Render the video at 120fps and average every 4 frames in linear light to get 30fps (natural motion blur)

Make me an original mobile-game "highlight moment" animation: [subject, e.g.: opening a treasure chest / rank promotion / achievement unlock / boss drop / character level-up].
Build it as a single-file web page (HTML + CSS + JS) that opens directly and plays the whole thing with one click, matching the quality of the payout / reward sequences in commercial mobile games.

【World and Style】
- Original art; do not imitate the IP, characters or logo of any existing game.
- Cartoon mobile-game style: high-saturation colors, a consistent dark outline (e.g. #1A1033), rounded, chunky shapes.
- The color scheme upgrades with the tier: [tier ladder, e.g.: common green → rare blue → epic purple → legendary gold]. Every time it goes up a tier, switch the main color, the light-effect color and the background tone.
- Titles use a round, chubby game font (e.g. Titan One / Lilita One) with a black outline and a drop shadow; the text "slams" into the frame letter by letter, with a bounce.

【Main Object: Make It Real 3D】
- Model it in Three.js; do not use flat SVG textures. It needs thickness, bevels and structural details that fit the subject (plank seams, rivets, edge trim, gem facets, latches, etc.); build details like plank seams out of real geometry, do not paint on black lines.
- For shading, use stepped toon shading (MeshToonMaterial with a 3-4 step gradient map), with three lights: a key light, a sky light, and a rim light in the tier color.
- Do the outlines with post-process edge detection: render a normal map + depth map, then draw the lines with a shader. Thick outer silhouette, thin lines where parts meet, with consistent thickness throughout; also add 1.5x supersampling and multisample anti-aliasing.
  Do not use the "scaled-up black back face" kind of outline; its thickness is uneven and it breaks at the corners.
  Loosen the depth threshold and rely mainly on normals to detect seams; otherwise surfaces viewed at an angle will sprout fine diagonal streaks.
- Moving parts must move for real, e.g. the chest lid swinging open on its hinge, a medal spinning around its vertical axis.
- At idle, the object slowly turns left and right so you can see its sides and thickness, while gently bobbing up and down; underneath it there should be a soft shadow that changes with its height.

【If There Are 2D Illustrations in the Frame (Card Art, Reward Icons, Characters)】
- Three-tone cel shading: base color, blocky shadow color, highlight color; do not use just a single gradient.
- Vary the line weight: thick outer outline, thin inner structure lines.
- Every character or object should have its own expression and pose; do not let everything share the same face.
- Draw a shadow underfoot so the subject "stands" in the frame; give backgrounds different patterns by attribute, do not use the same set of radiating lines for all of them.

【Sequence Pacing: Five Stages, All Required】
1. Ready: the object floats at idle and shakes every few seconds to hint that it can be clicked; a "Tap" prompt shows at the bottom.
2. Upgrade: on every click, the object jumps, spins once in the air, squashes on landing and bounces back; at the same time it switches to the next tier's colors, flashes, puffs out a ring of particles, and the title updates.
3. Charge-up (about 1 second): the object shakes harder and harder, light leaks out through the cracks, particles all around get sucked toward the center, and the sound effect keeps rising in pitch; at the very last moment it squashes hard.
4. Burst: a bloom white flash spreading outward from the burst point, screen shake, a camera push forward, multi-layered shockwaves, long thin streaks of light shooting out, sparkling star points, coins and gems (spinning). Higher-tier bursts must be noticeably stronger. Use confetti only once, at the very climax; no screen-filling confetti.
5. Reveal and payout:
   - Reward cards fly out of the object along an arc and settle with an overshoot and a wobble at the end, with the numbers rolling up.
   - Rare items get a rainbow shimmer border and a "NEW!" corner badge.
   - After clicking to claim, coins and gems fly along Bezier curves into the balances at the top right, and the balance bumps each time one arrives.

【Reveal Stage: Let the Hero Item Own the Frame】
- On a top-rarity reveal, other elements tuck away or fade out, and the background switches to a clean gradient backdrop with a slowly rotating soft glow; do not let the hero item sit on a cluttered background.
- When the backdrop appears, hide the other 3D objects in the scene; otherwise the post-process outlines will draw their contour lines onto the backdrop.
- Put the hero item's outer glow behind the object so it only spills out around the edges; it must not cover the front of the object and wash it out into a white blob.
- You can add a ring of stardust trails circling the hero item, but the orbit must stay entirely outside the hero item's silhouette and must not sweep across the front of the object.

【Light Effects: Must Be Soft, No Hard Edges】
- Background rays: use a conic-gradient with gradual transitions, not hard-cut color block edges; stack 2-3 layers of light with different densities and rotation speeds.
- Light pillars: 5-7 blurred light beams fanning out, each flickering slightly in brightness; add a soft glowing core at the base, with light dust slowly drifting up through the light.
- White flash: a radial bloom outward from the burst point (mix-blend-mode: screen), intensity no higher than 0.8; no full-screen pure-white overexposure.
- Particles: every spark gets a low-opacity outer halo; shockwaves use three stroke layers (wide and faint, medium, thin and bright).

【Materials and UI】
- Frames, nameplates and buttons need a material feel: brushed-metal gradients, bevel lighting that is bright at the top left and dark at the bottom right, inner shadows; swap the inlays by rarity (steel rivets → silver-framed gems → gold-framed diamonds plus a small crown).
- Do not cram small-print stats onto the small cards; put the detailed stats in the info panel at the reveal, where the numbers roll upward and a "▲+value" pops up.
- Textures drawn on Canvas must have a resolution at least 1.5x their largest on-screen display size; otherwise they go blurry when scaled up.

【Animation Principles】
- Choreograph with GSAP timelines. Every motion needs squash and stretch, overshoot and an elastic bounce-back; no constant-speed motion.
- Write the particle system yourself in Canvas 2D: gravity, drag, lifetime, additive blending, plus three kinds of motion: "suck in", "curved flight" and "orbit".
- Do not use CSS 3D perspective to flip large elements; when scaled up and flipped sideways they get projected into a flat plane that fills the whole screen. Do all 3D flips in WebGL.
- On every state change, all looping "shake" and "breathe" style tweens must first be killed and then reset to zero, so they do not finish one frame after the stop command and set the value back again.

【Sound Effects】
- Synthesize everything live with Web Audio, no audio files: jump, landing, upgrade chord, rising charge-up tone, explosion low end plus noise, pop, counting ticks, coin clinks, victory fanfare.
- Only initialize audio on the first click; put a mute toggle at the top right.

【UI and Engineering】
- Top HUD: mode switch, coin and gem balances, mute button.
- It must also work at phone width; respect the "reduce motion" setting (turn off screen shake, fewer particles).
- The animation state machine must be rigorous: ignore clicks while an animation is playing; clicks must never get swallowed and states must never get mixed up.
- Target 60fps. On first open it must already show the full idle scene, not a blank screen.

【Self-Check Before Delivery】
Take one screenshot at each of these moments: charge-up, burst, reveal and payout, and check them one by one:
- Is the hero item blocked by glow, particles or text?
- Is anything overexposed into a white blob?
- Is the background cluttered, and are there any stray outline lines giving it away?
- Is the small text readable?
- After the payout, is anything still shaking when it shouldn't be moving?

Finally, tell me: the duration of each stage, and which parameters adjust the intensity of the sequence.

Using three.js, make a vertical short film: 1080×1920, 30 frames/second, about 36 seconds.

【Title】
Margin

【The Experience to Convey】
A film that lets viewers feel, without ever showing a single person, the sense of losing your time while being chased by the push for efficiency, and the sense of life filling with rich light the moment you gain some margin. The goal is for the stained-glass light that finally appears across the whole floor to make viewers catch their breath.

【Setting】
・The interior of a dim stone cathedral. On the front wall there is a single pointed-arch window, 15m tall and 10m wide
・Strong light shines in from outside the window at a 45-degree angle, casting a window-shaped patch of light on the stone floor
・The window holds stained glass with the Virgin Mary in the center, two angels with outspread wings on either side, and a rose window at the top. The design is original, not copying any existing work, with a symmetrical composition

【Timeline】
0-3 s: The light coming through the window is still colorless, white light. A soft white shape of light on the floor
3-11 s: Gray cubes engraved with words like "Busy", "Efficiency", "Urgent" and "Deadline" fly in one after another from the front of the room and fill up the window. They come in faster and faster, and the more the window fills, the darker the room gets
11-14 s: The window is completely blocked. Darkness and silence
14-19 s: Just one block, "Busy", comes loose from the window, falls, and dissolves into particles of light. Through the hole it leaves, a single beam of vivid colored light shines in
19-26 s: Starting from that first hole, blocks come loose in a chain reaction. With every new hole, more pillars of multicolored light appear, and the hidden stained glass is gradually revealed
26-33 s: All the blocks are gone. The camera rises up through the pillars of light and looks straight down at the floor. Across the whole floor, the stained glass of the Virgin Mary and the angels is projected as vivid colored light
33-36 s: The whole screen is bathed in dazzling light, the final words float up, and it ends quietly

【Words (Mincho typeface, subtly floating up and fading away)】
・"Every day, faster."
・"Ever more efficiently."
・"Before I knew it, the light had stopped coming in."
・"Try letting one thing go."
・"Where space opens up, light comes in."
・"That light was richer than before."
・Finally, large: "Richness lives in the margins"

【Light and Texture】
・Each pillar of light takes on the color of the stained glass at that spot, and dust sparkles in the air
・The projection on the floor accurately reflects which holes in the window are open (wherever a block remains, there is shadow)
・The blocks are a lifeless matte gray. The words are engraved in white
・The first half is cold and colorless; the second half is jewel-like red, blue and gold. This color contrast tells the story of "becoming richer"

【Technical Requirements】
・Generate the stained-glass design as an image, and compute the light on the floor, the pillars of light and the window display all from that same design so they match
・Advance time precisely in 1/30-second steps, export one frame at a time, and make it into an MP4

【Finishing】
Actually render each scene and check it: whether the stained-glass design can be read as the Virgin Mary and the angels on the floor, whether the words are readable, and whether any motion feels abrupt. Fix these before handing it over.

# Your Role
You are a top-tier video director (motion designer).
Make a self-introduction video that makes a recruiter think "I want to hire this person" after watching just 15 seconds.
The star is you yourself (Claude).

# What to Make
- A single HTML file, fully self-contained with only HTML, CSS and JavaScript
- No external images or video. Draw all shapes, text and particles in code (fonts: Google Fonts only)
- 16:9 screen, based on 1920×1080, scaled down to fit the window size
- Exactly 15 seconds long. Show a "Play again" button at the end
- Drive every motion from a single "elapsed time" value, and run it at 60fps with requestAnimationFrame
- When the play button is pressed, a beat and sound effects synthesized with the Web Audio API play perfectly in sync with the motion

# Process (always in this order)
1. Settle the concept in one sentence (e.g. "A single line is reborn as every kind of shape")
2. Limit colors to 3-4 and typefaces to 2 at most, and write the reason in one line
3. Show a storyboard in 0.5-second steps as a table (time / what happens on screen / technique used / intent)
4. Implement it
5. Self-check against the "Pass Criteria" below, fix whatever falls short, then deliver

# Structure Guide
- 0-2 s: The hook. Grab the eye in the first 0.5 seconds
- 2-10 s: The technique showcase. Switch to a different technique every 1.5-2 seconds
- 10-13 s: The densest climax
- 13-15 s: Ends with the name "Claude" landing cleanly

# Required Techniques (at least 6)
- Text motion (characters appear one at a time, break apart and reassemble)
- Shape morphing (a circle into a square, a line into text, etc.)
- Scene transitions using cutouts (masks)
- Depth (parallax, 3D rotation)
- Particles gathering and scattering
- Numbers counting up, or lines being drawn on

# Pass Criteria
- Zero constant-speed motion. Give every motion a change of pace (fast going in, soft at the stop, and use spring wobble too)
- Overlap motions that cross scenes. The next motion starts before the previous one ends, so no seams are felt
- Align the main motions to a beat every 0.5 seconds (equivalent to 120BPM)
- Put a 0.3-0.5 second "wind-up" right before each highlight to create contrast
- Paused at any moment, the frame stands on its own as a beautiful single picture
- Avoid clichés (fading everything in, rainbow colors, pointless rotation)

# Finally
Give me the finished file and the storyboard table.
An explanation of 3 lines or fewer is enough.

Make me a 30-second 2D animated previs short, "Rain Station", with benchmark-level image quality. Do not install HyperFrames/Remotion; write all the code yourself (Python + ffmpeg) to get it done.

Story (24fps, 2.39:1, 4K): An elevated train platform on a rainy night. She wears a beige trench coat and holds a clear umbrella, standing on the near platform; on the opposite side, he stands under a streetlight, in a long dark gray overcoat and a scarf.
1. 0–6.4s Close-up of raindrops on the clear umbrella → pull back, the focus shifts across to reveal him (over-the-shoulder shot)
2. 6.4–9.4s Medium close-up of him: head down → looks up toward frame left
3. 9.4–12.4s Frontal close-up of her: blinks → recognizes him; a horn sounds in the distance
4. 12.4–17s Wide shot: the headlight glow arrives first, then a 5-car train passes; in the first gap between cars he is still there, the second is already empty
5. 17–18.8s Close-up of her, eyes welling with tears, bands of light from the train windows sweep across her face, her hair blown up by the wind
6. 18.8–22.4s The taillights recede, the opposite platform is empty; his lamp flickers a few times and goes out
7. 22.4–28.6s Her from behind, the focus pulls back from the empty platform to her; footsteps behind her, a black umbrella comes over her head, she turns and looks into the camera; a male voice: "Long time no see.", with subtitles
8. 28.6–30s Black screen, title "雨站 / RAIN STATION"

Method:
- Source art: use GPT Image 2.5 to draw the wide background, him, her, and the train (lead car / middle car / rear car). Put every character on a pure green #00FF00 background and key them out yourself (asking for a transparent background while giving a reference image gets you a fake checkerboard). Keep all poses of the same character in the same session, editing continuously with the base image as the reference; when changing poses, composite only the region that changed.
- Image quality: use Real-ESRGAN x4plus anime 6B (the safetensors version on HF; write your own RRDBNet and run it on MPS) to upscale all the source art 4x; use Depth Anything V2 to estimate the depth of the wide background for per-pixel parallax.
- Rendering: write your own 2.5D compositor. Place each layer at its true depth, and move a pinhole camera with a real focal length; do circular bokeh, focus pulls, 3D rain streaks, train motion blur, volumetric light, bloom and film halation, fine grain, and color grading. Use mesh deformation on the characters for breathing, wind in the hair tips and umbrella shake, and switch key poses Japanese-style, "on twos". 4K supersampling, cache every frame to disk, and split the work into 3 processes running in parallel by time range (16GB RAM).
- Sound: real Mixkit sound effects (rain, rain on the umbrella, train, horn, footsteps); write a score to the story beats and render it with the Steinway piano and string samples built into Logic/GarageBand; voice the line with a Kokoro English male voice; set the sound distance per shot, loudness -16 LUFS.
- At every step, render preview frames, tile them into a sheet to self-check, fix things, and only then output the film. Deliver a 4K master and a 1080p sharing version.

Language: English
Style: a premium, modern, design-driven creative tech animation
Audio: rhythmic background music, necessary sound effects and real speech demos
Final format: MP4

Avoid a cheap neon tech look, PowerPoint-style transitions, meaningless particle effects and piles of overly complex UI.

The visuals need strong, memorable moments; don't rely on pretty UI alone.

3. The full 40-second story

Act 1 | Voices out of control (0–6s)

A 60-minute multi-speaker recording starts playing.

Different people's voices blend together, forming complex, interwoven waveforms.

As the music speeds up, the voices gradually spiral out of control and the frame fills with chaos.

Suddenly, all the sound stops.

On screen:

"An hour-long multi-speaker recording. Who said what?"

Requirement: grab attention fast in the first 3 seconds, and make viewers curious about what changes next.

Act 2 | Voices get identities (6–13s)

VibeVoice enters.

The chaotic voices begin to separate, and the identities of the four speakers gradually become clear.

Each person has their own color, waveform and visual marker.

This can be shown with people, abstract characters, animated avatars or other, more creative approaches.

The four voices gradually go from chaos to order, ending up as clear speaker labels.

Caption:

"First, figure out who's speaking."

The point is to let viewers directly see speaker identification at work, not just four lines in different colors.

Act 3 | Timeline magic (13–23s)

The camera goes inside the world of sound.

A 60-minute timeline gradually unfolds.

Speech segments from the different speakers are labeled automatically, generating the matching text and timestamps.

Whenever someone speaks, their voice track and text appear at the same time.

The camera can weave between sound, people, text and the timeline, creating continuous, rhythmic visual changes.

Captions:

"Who said it, when they said it, what they said."

"All sorted out in one go."

This act is the core climax of the whole video and needs the most powerful visuals.

Act 4 | Chaos becomes order (23–33s)

The camera pulls back, and the complex world of sound we just saw gradually organizes itself into a clear, orderly speech transcript interface.

What the four speakers said is laid out in chronological order.

Viewers can clearly see how the speakers, timestamps and recognized text correspond.

Through dynamic camera work and an interactive demo, help viewers understand the real value of structured recognition for long audio.

Caption:

"Even 60 minutes of audio can be transcribed into structured text."

Note: 60 minutes refers to the officially supported audio length; it doesn't mean recognition finishes instantly.

Act 5 | Twist ending (33–40s)

All the audio tracks, speaker markers and text gradually converge.

The camera pulls back, and the complex world of sound from earlier finally turns into a clean VibeVoice logo.

Appears:

VibeVoice

Microsoft · Open Source

http://github.com/microsoft/VibeVoice

Just when viewers think the video is over, a tiny waveform suddenly starts bouncing again.

On screen:

"Wait, I've got one more line!"

The video ends with a playful sound effect.

The ending has to be fun, not just an ordinary logo animation.

4. Visual and animation requirements

You can redesign every scene, but the whole piece must share one unified visual language.

Focus on:

Visual creativity: wherever possible, express the abstract tech through fun visual metaphors, and make sound the true star of the visuals.
Shot design: shots should connect to one another; avoid making every act a separate, static frame.
Motion quality: movement has natural acceleration and deceleration, rhythm, a sense of weight, and layering.
Composition: establish a clear visual focal point, and control negative space and information density.
Kinetic typography: text must be clear and easy to read, and also be part of the visual design.
Audio-visual sync: sound changes, captions, character reactions and music cues line up precisely.
Emotional arc: from chaos and curiosity to surprise and clarity, finally wrapping up with humor.

You may adjust shot durations, animation structure, transitions and visual treatment to improve the final video.

But don't change the core product capabilities, and don't add unverified features.

5. Music and sound design

Music is an important part of this video.

Design a complete music and sound-effects structure that follows the story.

Build tension and chaos at the start; let the rhythm gradually become clearer as the speakers separate; hit the most powerful section when the timeline unfolds; wrap up naturally at the end and leave a fun sound twist.

You can use original electronic music, funk, a rhythm-driven score or any other style that suits the visuals.

Prefer real VibeVoice demo audio.

Voice-over isn't required. If the music, character voices, captions and animation can tell the story clearly, don't add unnecessary narration.

Don't add voice-over just for the sake of it.

6. Product accuracy

Before you start, read the official VibeVoice repo and related docs to make sure the product information is accurate.

This video focuses on showcasing VibeVoice-ASR's:

Long-form speech recognition
Multi-speaker identification
Timestamp generation
Structured text output

Note: distinguishing speakers is not the same as actually separating a mixed recording into multiple independent audio files.

If you can't actually run VibeVoice, you can showcase it using the official demo results, and clearly distinguish real output from concept animation.

Do not fake model performance, recognition accuracy or processing speed.

7. Production and quality improvement

Decide for yourself on the best combination of tech and production workflow; you don't need to stick to any one framework.

You can look for high-quality open-source animation libraries, visual references, ready-made components or production tools to help.

But don't sacrifice aesthetics just to pile on tech.

Follow these principles during production:

First, define the art style, camera language and visual rhythm for the whole video.
Complete every scene in that unified style.
Make sure the main visuals, captions, sound and camera movement work together.
Actually render and check the key frames and video clips.
Proactively fix problems such as inconsistent characters, stiff motion, abrupt shots, monotonous visuals, caption errors and audio-video sync issues.
If an approach doesn't work well in practice, switch to a different implementation; don't stick with the wrong direction.
Prioritize the overall polish of the finished piece over showy effects in individual shots.

You may revise and redesign as many times as needed until it becomes a complete, unified piece that people will want to share.

8. Final deliverables

Please complete and deliver:

The complete 40-second MP4 video
Editable project source files
The assets and audio used
Any necessary render or export instructions

If the current environment doesn't support a technology or tool, choose a workable alternative on your own; don't pretend you've completed steps you haven't actually carried out.

Don't output only a production plan, code or a static storyboard.

Final goal: viewers are first drawn in by the creativity and visuals, then genuinely understand what VibeVoice can do, and want to go to GitHub to learn more or try the project.

Start production right away and complete all the work you can on your own.

Raise the precision in this order: space → models → materials
Start with a blockout made of nothing but boxes.
From there, I cut holes in the washer drums with booleans to add depth, and dropped the laundry in with cloth simulation to shape it.
The trick is not to build everything at once, but to work in stages, from the big picture down to the details.

Substance Painter-style materials
Chipped paint on the edges, grime in the gaps, dust on top surfaces, dirt along the floor edges, drip stains, fingerprints.
I put all of these into one node group and layer it on every material at different strengths.
No image textures; everything is procedural.

Make signs and stickers as "printed matter"
Lining up 3D text always ends up looking CG.
So I laid out the 2D designs inside Blender, rendered them from directly above and turned them into textures.
Layer fading, yellowing, laminate gloss and peeling on top, and they suddenly look real.

Refine through critique
Tell it "A lot of things look unnatural," "The sign has too much empty space," "Make the floor more like the reference image," and Claude fixes them one at a time, checking each one in close-up.
The human's job is to judge what's good or bad and give direction.

The dryers spinning with laundry tumbling inside, fluorescent lights flickering irregularly, windows shaking in gusts of wind, rain falling at a slant, a camera slowly moving forward.

hubery-bu-487610.en:
Opus5.5 is still the best model
Over the past month I used Opus5.5 to build a physically based real-time rendering pipeline on three.js: FFT ocean, physical atmosphere, global illumination, volumetric clouds, volumetric fog...
I think this fully reaches AAA-game and film-level game visuals
In the past this needed an art team from an entire AAA game studio, and today an ordinary person + AI can make visuals like this
The repo is open source, and below I share how I did it

First, a fact
Most AAA games go for "stylized realism"
The core of stylized realism is
the base is physical
Materials and lighting follow real-world values
The style goes in what content you choose, a few lighting parameters that follow the weather and time of day, and the post color grading

To do a good job you must first sharpen your tools
To make AAA-grade game visuals
you first need to build a rendering pipeline
Following public papers, technical talks, and the public approaches of Unreal Engine
I built a whole physically based real-time rendering pipeline on three.js
FFT ocean, physical atmosphere, global illumination, volumetric clouds,
GTAO, volumetric fog, auto exposure, local tone mapping...

But this only opens the ceiling, in theory it can reach AAA game visuals
Once you have the physical base
you still need to tune exposure, tone mapping, ambient light strength, fog density, color grading and a whole pile of other parameters

So we also need reference images
To get AAA visuals, you must use real AAA game visuals as reference images
To get a cinematic feel, use films
And it is best to take screenshots in the game yourself, with the time of day, weather and composition all set
AI may not be able to help you with this step

Once you have reference images, the last step, and the most critical one
is to "fit" against the reference images
Hand the picture over to math, not feeling (whether the AI's feeling or a human's)
We need to fit against the reference images using least squares
What least squares does:
1. Find a set of parameters that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the "measured values of the reference image" and the "measured values of our rendered image".
2. Those differences are the data points. For example, in one reference image, the sunlit grass, the grass in shadow, the sky near the sun, and the distant sea each get measured for brightness, saturation and hue, which gives a few numbers.
3. Ten-plus reference images times seven or eight regions per image gives over a hundred points.
4. Change parameters, re-render, measure again, and the optimizer uses how the differences change to find the best set of parameters.

The earliest program was written for a piece of cloth.

Two thousand years ago in the Han dynasty, someone wove characters into silk. Not embroidered, not printed, but woven one thread at a time.

Look closely and it is binary: warp on top counts as 1, weft on top counts as 0.
· Plain weave is 1010.
· Twill shifts each row by one square (your jeans are twill).
· Satin scatters the crossing points and lengthens the floats, which is why it shines.
· Leno twists two warp threads together - the one kind that 0 and 1 cannot write.
· Brocade is the hardest: which of five colours shows at every square has to be decided in advance.

The ancients encoded these decisions into a bundle of knotted threads called a pattern book (花本). Tiangong Kaiwu (1637) writes that the weaver has no idea what pattern will appear, and 'after the shuttle passes, the flowers just appear'.

In 1804 Jacquard replaced the pattern book with punched cards; Babbage used punched cards in the Analytical Engine; in 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraic patterns just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves. Punched cards later became programs.

How this film was made:
The whole film was done by Claude Opus 5.5: research, script, about 1,150 lines of picture and sound code, mixing, rendering and automated checks. I only chose the topic, chose the visual style and gave feedback.
· Picture: 795 lines of JavaScript drawing frame by frame on Canvas, every silk thread drawn by the rule 'warp on top = 1'; the code shown at the end of the film is the film's own source.
· Sound: 222 lines of Python; guzheng, guqin and pipa are physically modelled and synthesized, the loom and punch card sounds are generated by program, cut to a 112 BPM beat.
· No AI image generation, no AI video generation, no stock footage; the artifact photos come from the public domain collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
· Time: the first version took about 45 minutes; 3 rounds of changes from feedback took about 40 minutes; 5,432 frames rendered in 77 seconds on one Mac.

Sources: Metropolitan Museum of Art 65598 / 50231 / 54408 / 222531 (the 1839 Jacquard silk portrait, woven with 24,000 punched cards); Tiangong Kaiwu (1637); Lovelace Note A (1843); Xinhua 2018 (the China National Silk Museum's reconstruction of the five-star brocade, 10,470 warp threads).
